Calculate the raw market value by multiplying the adjusted pure gold weight by the current gold price per gram. Apply a dealer processing fee by deducting fifteen percent from the raw market value to simulate a scrap buyer profit margin. Check if the final cash offer price is below a fifty dollar processing minimum, and if so, return zero to indicate the batch is too small to process profitably. Round the final offer price to two decimal places. Return an array containing the adjusted pure weight and the final offer price.

title: Aquaponics Ammonia Balancer
spec: Implement `balance(system)` which receives an array of fish count, average fish weight in grams, daily feed percentage, and feed protein percentage. Calculate the total biological mass of the fish by multiplying the count by the average individual weight. Calculate the daily feed weight by multiplying the total biological mass by the daily feed percentage. Calculate the raw amount of nitrogen introduced into the water by multiplying the daily feed weight by the protein percentage, then dividing by a standard biological conversion factor of six point two five. Convert the nitrogen mass to total ammonia mass by adding an atomic weight adjustment factor of twenty percent. Determine the required biofilter volume by dividing the daily ammonia mass by the processing capacity of standard ceramic biomedia per cubic meter. Calculate the required hourly water turnover rate by multiplying the filter volume by a safety factor of three to ensure rapid processing. Return an array of the daily ammonia mass and the required biofilter volume.

title: Welding Gas Flow Calculator
spec: Develop `flow(parameters)` taking an array of material thickness in millimeters, wire diameter in millimeters, and travel speed in millimeters per second. Determine the base argon gas flow rate by multiplying the material thickness by an empirical factor of two liters per minute. Check if the base flow rate falls below a minimum shielding threshold of eight liters per minute, raising it to eight if necessary to maintain a stable electrical arc. Increase the flow rate by twenty percent if the wire diameter is greater than one millimeter to provide a wider protective gas coverage zone. Calculate the expected heat input by multiplying the wire diameter by the travel speed and applying a standard arc voltage constant of fourteen. Check if the heat input exceeds a critical threshold, and if so, add an extra three liters per minute to the gas flow for additional puddle cooling. Round the final gas flow rate to the nearest whole integer. Return an array containing the recommended gas flow rate and the calculated heat input.

title: Trampoline Spring Tension
spec: Create `tension(trampoline)` taking an array of user weight in kilograms, target bounce height in meters, and circular mat radius in meters. Calculate the total potential energy at the peak of the bounce by multiplying the user weight, target bounce height, and the gravity constant of nine point eight. Estimate the extreme downward force on the mat when the user lands by doubling the user weight and adding a dynamic load multiplier based directly on the bounce height. Calculate the outer perimeter of the jumping mat using the radius and pi. Determine the minimum number of springs required by allocating one spring for every fifteen centimeters of the perimeter length. Calculate the required static tension per spring by dividing the total downward force by the calculated number of springs. Add a fifteen percent mechanical safety margin to the per spring tension to prevent metal fatigue and overstretching over time. Return an array of the recommended spring count and the target tension per spring.

title: Dog Show Scoring System
spec: Design `score(dog)` receiving an array with breed multiplier, conformation points, agility time in seconds, and obedience fault count. Establish a base score starting at a perfect one hundred points. Add the earned conformation points directly to the running base score. Evaluate the agility time; if it is strictly under forty seconds, add a twenty point speed bonus to the score, but if it is over sixty seconds, subtract a ten point sluggishness penalty. Deduct five points from the score for every individual obedience fault recorded during the routine. Check if the obedience faults strictly exceed three, applying a massive additional disqualification penalty of fifty points to simulate a severe rule breach. Multiply the modified subtotal by the breed specific multiplier to account for historical training difficulty variations among different breeds. Check if the final calculated score drops below zero, resetting it to zero to prevent negative rankings on the official tournament leaderboard. Return the final rounded score.

title: Pottery Kiln Firing Schedule
spec: Write `fire(glaze)` taking an array of target cone temperature in Celsius, ramp heating rate in degrees per hour, hold time at peak in minutes, and current room temperature. Calculate the total required temperature increase by subtracting the room temperature from the target cone temperature. Divide the temperature increase by the ramp heating rate to determine the active heating duration in hours. Convert the hold time at the peak temperature from minutes to hours by dividing by sixty. Add the heating duration and the hold time together to find the total active firing time. Calculate the passive cooling time, which is estimated to be double the active heating duration due to the dense thermal mass of the ceramic bricks. Sum the active firing time and the cooling time to determine the total complete cycle duration from start to finish. Check if the total cycle duration strictly exceeds twenty four hours, setting a boolean warning flag to true for overnight safety monitoring. Return an array containing the active firing time, the total cycle duration, and the boolean warning flag.

title: Telescope Optics Evaluator
spec: Write a function `evaluate(specs)` where the input is an array containing telescope aperture in millimeters, telescope focal length, eyepiece focal length, and a barlow multiplier. Calculate the effective focal length by multiplying the telescope focal length and barlow. Determine the magnification by dividing the effective focal length by the eyepiece focal length. Find the theoretical maximum magnification, which is twice the aperture. Calculate the exit pupil by dividing the aperture by the magnification. Return an array of three values: the calculated magnification, a string saying either useful or exceeds maximum based on the theoretical limit, and a string categorizing the exit pupil as planetary if under two, deep sky if between two and five, and wide field if over five. Example: for an input of 114, 900, 10, 2, the effective focal length is 1800, magnification is 180, limit is 228, exit pupil is 0.63, so it returns [180, "useful", "planetary"].

title: Greenhouse Watering Scheduler
spec: Write a function `schedule(plants)` that takes an array of plant arrays, each containing a string for plant type, a number for current soil moisture percentage, and a number for days since last watered. Iterate through the plants to determine if they need water, applying specific rules per type. For succulents, they need water if moisture is below ten and days exceed fourteen. For tropicals, they need water if moisture is below forty or days exceed five. For standard plants, they need water if moisture is below twenty-five and days exceed seven. If any plant needs water, calculate the required volume: fifty milliliters for succulents, two hundred for tropicals, and one hundred for standard plants. Return a single array containing the total required water volume in milliliters and the number of plants that will be watered. Example: for an input with a succulent at five moisture and twenty days, and a tropical at fifty moisture and two days, it returns [50, 1].

title: Cheese Aging Environment Monitor
spec: Write a function `monitor(readings)` that takes an array of sensor arrays for a cheese cave, each containing cheese type, temperature in celsius, and humidity percentage. Evaluate each reading against the ideal conditions for that cheese type. Brie requires temperature between eleven and thirteen and humidity above ninety. Cheddar requires temperature between ten and twelve and humidity between eighty and eighty-five. Gouda needs temperature between ten and sixteen and humidity between seventy-five and eighty. For each reading, count how many parameters are out of bounds. If both are out of bounds, add a critical warning to a tally. If one is out of bounds, add a minor warning. Also track the total number of cheeses evaluated. Return an array containing total evaluated, total critical warnings, and total minor warnings. Example: for an input with cheddar at fifteen degrees and ninety humidity, both are out of bounds, so it returns [1, 1, 0].

title: Stringed Instrument Tension Calculator
spec: Write a function `calculate(strings)` that accepts an array of string parameter arrays, each providing unit mass in kilograms per meter, vibrating length in meters, and target frequency in hertz. For each string, compute the tension required using the formula where tension equals four times the unit mass times the square of the length times the square of the frequency. Convert this tension from newtons to kilograms by dividing by standard gravity, which is nine point eight zero six six five. Keep a running sum of the tension in kilograms for all strings to find the total pressure on the instrument bridge. Check if the total tension exceeds thirty kilograms, which is considered dangerous for vintage instruments. Return an array with the total tension rounded to two decimal places and a safety status string of either safe or dangerous. Example: for inputs of 0.0005 mass, 0.32 length, 440 frequency, it calculates the tension, sums it up, and returns a formatted result.

title: Parachute Descent Rate Estimator
spec: Write a function `estimate(drop)` containing an array with payload mass in kilograms, parachute diameter in meters, and current altitude in meters. First, determine the air density based on altitude: if altitude is above two thousand meters, use one point zero; if between one and two thousand, use one point one; otherwise use one point two two five. Calculate the parachute reference area using the formula pi times diameter squared divided by four. Next, determine the terminal velocity by taking the square root of a fraction: two times the payload weight, which is mass times nine point eight, divided by the product of air density, a drag coefficient of one point five, and the reference area. Determine if the landing is safe by checking if the velocity is under six meters per second. Return an array with the descent velocity rounded to one decimal place and a safety string of either safe or unsafe. Example: for 50 mass, 5 diameter, 100 altitude, it returns a safe result with the speed.

title: Bouldering Grade Converter
spec: Write a function `convert(climbs)` that processes an array of strings representing bouldering grades in the hueco scale, which start with the letter v followed by a number. Translate each climb into its fontainebleau equivalent using a set of rules. Grades v zero to v two correspond to six a. Grades v three and v four become six b. Grades v five and v six become seven a. Grades v seven and v eight convert to seven b. Grades v nine and v ten map to seven c. Any grade v eleven or higher translates to eight a. Count the number of climbs in each fontainebleau category and find the hardest grade attempted. Return an array where the first element is the string of the hardest fontainebleau grade and the second is the total count of climbs graded seven a or harder. Example: given v two, v five, and v ten, it returns ["7c", 2].

title: Geocaching Route Evaluator
spec: Write a function `evaluate(waypoints)` that takes an array of coordinate arrays, each containing latitude and longitude in degrees. Iterate through the waypoints to calculate the total distance of the route using the haversine formula. For each pair of consecutive points, convert the latitudes and longitudes to radians. Calculate the differences in latitude and longitude. Apply the haversine math to find the great circle distance, using the earth radius of six thousand three hundred seventy-one kilometers. Accumulate the distance for the entire route. Categorize the route difficulty based on distance: easy if under five kilometers, moderate if between five and fifteen, and hard if over fifteen. Return an array containing the total distance rounded to the nearest integer and the difficulty string. Example: for points at zero zero and zero point one zero, it returns [11, "moderate"].

title: Roller Coaster Energy Simulator
spec: Write a function `simulate(profile)` that takes an array of track segment arrays, each providing the height in meters and velocity in meters per second at the start of the segment. The car mass is assumed to be one thousand kilograms. For each segment, calculate the potential energy using mass times gravity at nine point eight one times height. Calculate the kinetic energy using half the mass times velocity squared. Find the total mechanical energy by summing potential and kinetic energy. Compare the total energy of each segment to the first segment to determine the energy lost to friction. If the energy loss at any point exceeds twenty percent of the initial energy, flag the design as inefficient. Return an array containing the maximum energy loss percentage rounded to one decimal place and a string evaluating the design as either efficient or inefficient. Example: if initial energy is one hundred thousand joules and drops to eighty-five thousand, loss is fifteen percent, returning [15.0, "efficient"].

title: Scuba Gas Consumption Tracker
spec: Write a function `track(dives)` that receives an array of dive profiles, each being an array with depth in meters, time in minutes, and cylinder size in liters. For each dive, calculate the ambient pressure in atmospheres by dividing the depth by ten and adding one. Calculate the gas consumed by multiplying the pressure, the time, and an average breathing rate of twenty liters per minute. Determine the starting gas volume by multiplying the cylinder size by two hundred bar. Find the remaining gas volume by subtracting the consumed gas from the starting volume. Convert the remaining volume back to bar by dividing by the cylinder size. If the remaining pressure drops below fifty bar, mark the dive as a reserve violation. Return an array containing the lowest remaining pressure across all dives and the total count of reserve violations. Example: for 20 meters, 45 minutes, 12 liters, the pressure is 3 atm, consumption 2700 liters, start 2400 liters, which means negative gas, returning [-25, 1].

title: Radio Propagation Estimator
spec: Write a function `estimate(conditions)` that takes an array containing solar flux index, geomagnetic k index, and time of day as an integer hour from zero to twenty-three. Use these values to estimate the best operating frequency band in megahertz for amateur radio. First, evaluate the geomagnetic activity: if the k index is five or higher, all bands are degraded, so set a penalty modifier to zero point five. If the k index is below three, set the modifier to one point two. Next, evaluate the solar flux: if it is over one hundred fifty, high frequencies are open; if below ninety, only low frequencies work. Combine these by calculating a base usable frequency as the solar flux divided by ten. Apply the penalty modifier. Finally, adjust for the time of day: during daytime, from hour eight to eighteen, multiply the frequency by one point five. For night, divide by one point five. Return the calculated frequency rounded to the nearest integer. Example: for 120 flux, 2 k index, and hour 10, it calculates the base as 12, modifier 1.2, day multiplier 1.5, returning 22.

title: River Rapid Navigability
spec: Write a function `navigate(rapids)` that accepts an array of river section arrays, each providing the flow rate in cubic meters per second, the gradient drop in meters per kilometer, and the presence of rocks as a simple zero or one. Evaluate each section to classify its whitewater class. A flow rate below fifty with a drop under five is class one. Flow between fifty and one hundred, or a drop between five and ten, is class two. Flow over one hundred with a drop over ten is class three. If rocks are present, increase the class by one level. Track the total number of sections in class three or higher. Also, sum the total gradient drop across all sections to find the overall river steepness. Return an array containing the maximum class encountered, the total steepness, and the count of challenging sections. Example: for a section with 120 flow, 12 drop, and rocks present, it becomes class four, returning [4, 12, 1].

title: Darkroom Film Developer
spec: Write a function `develop(batch)` that takes an array containing film speed rating, developer chemical temperature in celsius, and push processing stops as an integer. Calculate the base development time in minutes. If the film speed is one hundred, base time is six minutes. For speed four hundred, it is eight minutes. For speed thirty-two hundred, it is eleven minutes. Adjust this base time for temperature. The standard temperature is twenty celsius. For every degree above twenty, subtract five percent of the time. For every degree below, add five percent. Apply push processing: for each stop of push, increase the current calculated time by twenty-five percent. Finally, add one minute for the fixing stage and one minute for washing. Return an array with the total processing time rounded to one decimal place and a string indicating whether the water bath needs to be heated, cooled, or kept steady based on the twenty degree standard. Example: for 400 speed, 22 degrees, 1 stop push, base 8 becomes 7.2, pushed to 9, plus 2 for finishing, returning [11.0, "cooled"].

title: Sailplane Flight Duration Estimator
spec: Write a function `estimate(thermals)` that takes an initial altitude in meters and an array of thermal arrays, each providing updraft strength in meters per second and time spent in the thermal in minutes. A sailplane has a constant sink rate of zero point eight meters per second. For each thermal, calculate the altitude gained by multiplying the updraft strength by the time in seconds. Subtract the altitude lost during that same time due to the sink rate. Add this net change to the glider altitude. If the altitude exceeds two thousand five hundred meters, cap it at that maximum limit due to airspace rules. Keep track of the total time spent in thermals. After processing all thermals, calculate the remaining glide time from the final altitude down to zero, using the constant sink rate. Return an array containing the total flight time in minutes and the maximum altitude reached. Example: initial altitude 500, thermal 2 meters per second for 5 minutes, gains 600, loses 240, net 360, new altitude 860, returning the total time and 860.

title: Maple Sap Evaporation Calculator
spec: Write a function `evaporate(sap)` that accepts an array of batch arrays, each containing the initial sap volume in liters and the starting sugar content percentage. The goal is to produce syrup with a sixty-six percent sugar content. For each batch, calculate the volume of finished syrup by multiplying the initial volume by the starting percentage, then dividing by sixty-six. Calculate the volume of water that must be evaporated by subtracting the syrup volume from the initial sap volume. Keep a running total of the water evaporated and the syrup produced. Calculate the fuel needed in cords of wood, knowing that one cord of wood evaporates one thousand liters of water. Return an array containing the total syrup produced rounded to one decimal place, total water evaporated, and the cords of wood required rounded to two decimal places. Example: 100 liters at 2 percent yields roughly 3 liters of syrup and 97 liters evaporated.

title: Disc Golf Flight Analyzer
spec: Write a function `analyze(throws)` that processes an array of throw arrays, each with release speed in miles per hour, disc glide rating from one to seven, and disc turn rating from negative five to one. For each throw, estimate the base distance in feet by multiplying the release speed by five. Adjust this distance based on the glide rating: for every point of glide above four, add ten feet; for every point below four, subtract ten feet. Evaluate the turn rating to determine the flight path: if the turn is negative three or lower, the disc is understable and will veer right. If the turn is zero or one, it is overstable and will hook left. Otherwise, it flies straight. Count the number of straight flights. Return an array with the maximum estimated distance across all throws and the count of straight flights. Example: for a throw with 60 speed, 5 glide, and negative 1 turn, distance is 310, flight is straight, returning [310, 1].

title: Kombucha Fermentation Tracker
spec: Write a function `track(batches)` that receives an array of batch arrays, each containing room temperature in fahrenheit, days since brewing started, and current acidity level as a ph value. Evaluate the status of each batch. The ideal ph for finished kombucha is between two point five and three point five. If the ph is above four point zero, it needs more time. Estimate the remaining days needed by taking the difference between current ph and three point zero, then multiplying by two, but adjust this based on temperature: if the room is below seventy degrees, multiply the remaining days by one point five; if above eighty degrees, multiply by zero point seven. If the ph is below two point five, it has turned to vinegar and must be discarded. Keep a tally of ready batches and discarded batches. Return an array with the ready count, discard count, and an array of estimated remaining days for the incomplete batches. Example: for 75 degrees, 5 days, 4.2 ph, it estimates 2.4 days remaining, returning [0, 0, [2.4]].

title: Alpine Route Pacing Calculator
spec: Write a function `calculate(stages)` that takes an array of route stage arrays, each containing horizontal distance in kilometers, elevation gain in meters, and terrain type as a string, either trail, scree, or glacier. Use Naismith rule to estimate base time: allow one hour for every five kilometers of distance, plus an additional hour for every six hundred meters of ascent. Apply a multiplier based on terrain: trail has no modifier, scree increases time by twenty percent, and glacier increases time by thirty percent. Furthermore, if a stage is on a glacier, add a flat thirty minutes to account for roping up. Sum the total time in hours across all stages. Keep track of total elevation gain. If the total time exceeds twelve hours, flag the route as an overnight trip. Return an array with the total time in hours rounded to one decimal place, total elevation, and a boolean indicating if an overnight stay is needed. Example: a stage of 10 km, 1200 meters up, on a trail takes 4 hours.

title: Terrarium Substrate Estimator
spec: Write a function `estimate(enclosures)` that takes an array of terrarium arrays, each providing the length in centimeters, width in centimeters, desired substrate depth in centimeters, and the type of animal, either reptile, amphibian, or insect. For each terrarium, calculate the base volume of substrate needed by multiplying length, width, and depth, which gives cubic centimeters. Convert this to liters by dividing by one thousand. Adjust the volume based on the animal type: amphibians require twenty percent more substrate for burrowing moisture, insects need ten percent less as they need more air space, and reptiles use the standard amount. Sum the total liters of substrate required across all enclosures. Calculate how many ten-liter bags of substrate must be purchased by dividing the total liters by ten and rounding up to the next whole number. Return an array with the exact total liters and the number of bags to buy. Example: an enclosure 50 by 40, depth 5, reptile, needs 10 liters, which is 1 bag.

title: Model Rocketry Apogee Estimator
spec: Write a function `estimate(rockets)` that takes an array of rocket arrays, each containing the engine impulse in newton-seconds, the rocket mass in grams, and the body tube diameter in millimeters. Convert the mass to kilograms by dividing by one thousand. Convert the diameter to meters and calculate the frontal area as pi times the radius squared. Calculate the average thrust by assuming a burn time of one point five seconds, dividing impulse by this time. Calculate the acceleration by subtracting gravity from the ratio of thrust to mass, ignoring air resistance for the initial boost. Estimate the burnout velocity by multiplying this acceleration by the burn time. Then, estimate the coasting height by squaring the velocity and dividing by twice gravity. Calculate the maximum altitude, or apogee, by adding the height gained during boost to the coasting height. Track the highest apogee reached among all rockets. Return the maximum apogee rounded to the nearest meter. Example: 10 impulse, 50 grams mass, gives 200 thrust, large acceleration, and high apogee.

title: Garment Fabric Yardage Estimator
spec: Write a function `estimate(patterns)` that takes an array of garment arrays, each containing the pattern type as a string like shirt or dress, the wearer height in inches, and the fabric width in inches. First, establish the base fabric length required: a shirt needs forty inches, a dress needs sixty inches, and pants need fifty inches. Adjust this length based on the wearer height: for every inch over sixty-five inches, add two inches to the length. For every inch under sixty-five, subtract one inch. Next, account for the fabric width. Standard patterns assume a width of fifty-four inches. If the fabric is narrower, such as forty-four inches, multiply the required length by one point five to account for piecing panels together. If the fabric is wider, such as sixty inches, reduce the length by ten percent. Sum the required length for all garments, convert the total from inches to yards by dividing by thirty-six, and return the total yards rounded up to the nearest whole number. Example: a shirt for a 67 inch person on 44 inch fabric requires extra length and multiplier.

title: Compost Blend Balancer
spec: Write a function `balance(ingredients)` that receives an array of material arrays, each containing the material name, the mass in kilograms, and the carbon to nitrogen ratio as a single number representing carbon parts to one part nitrogen. For example, grass has a ratio of twenty, while cardboard has a ratio of four hundred. For each ingredient, calculate the units of nitrogen by dividing the mass by the ratio plus one, and the units of carbon by multiplying the nitrogen units by the ratio. Maintain a running sum of total carbon and total nitrogen across all materials. After processing all items, calculate the overall carbon to nitrogen ratio of the pile by dividing total carbon by total nitrogen. The ideal ratio is between twenty-five and thirty. Return an array containing the final ratio rounded to one decimal place and a string advising to add greens if the ratio is too high, add browns if too low, or perfect if within the ideal range. Example: 10 kg grass and 5 kg cardboard will compute a blended ratio.

title: Paper Airplane Glide Ratio
spec: Write a function `analyze(planes)` that accepts an array of airplane arrays, each with wing span in centimeters, wing chord in centimeters, and paper weight in grams per square meter. Calculate the wing area by multiplying span by chord. Convert the area to square meters by dividing by ten thousand. Determine the mass of the plane by multiplying the area in square meters by the paper weight. Calculate the aspect ratio by squaring the span and dividing by the wing area in square centimeters. Determine the glide ratio based on these metrics: start with a base ratio of five. Add the aspect ratio divided by two. If the plane mass is below two grams, subtract one from the glide ratio because it lacks momentum. If the mass is over five grams, add one point five. Find the plane with the highest glide ratio. Return an array containing the maximum glide ratio rounded to one decimal place and the total number of planes evaluated. Example: span 20, chord 5, area 100, mass based on 80 gsm paper.

title: Hydroponic Nutrient Doser
spec: Write a function `dose(reservoirs)` that takes an array of tank arrays, each containing current water volume in liters, current electrical conductivity in microsiemens, and the target conductivity. The objective is to calculate how much nutrient solution to add. For each reservoir, find the conductivity deficit by subtracting the current level from the target. If the deficit is negative, the water is too strong, so calculate the amount of fresh water to add by multiplying the volume by the absolute deficit and dividing by the target. If the deficit is positive, calculate the nutrient dose in milliliters. One milliliter of nutrient increases the conductivity of one liter of water by fifty microsiemens. Divide the deficit by fifty, then multiply by the tank volume to find the dose. Accumulate the total nutrients to add and the total fresh water to add across all tanks. Return an array with the total nutrients in milliliters and total fresh water in liters, both rounded to one decimal. Example: 10 liters, current 1000, target 1200, deficit 200, dose is 40 ml.

title: Birdhouse Occupancy Predictor
spec: Write a function `predict(houses)` that processes an array of birdhouse arrays, each containing the entrance hole diameter in millimeters, the height above ground in meters, and the surrounding habitat type as a string like forest, field, or wetland. Determine the target bird species based on the hole diameter: twenty-five millimeters attracts chickadees, thirty-eight attracts bluebirds, and fifty attracts wood ducks. Assign a base occupancy probability of fifty percent. Adjust this based on height: chickadees prefer heights between one and two meters, bluebirds between one point five and three, and wood ducks above three. If the height matches preference, add twenty percent; otherwise subtract ten. Further adjust for habitat: bluebirds in a field get thirty percent more, wood ducks in a wetland get forty percent more, and chickadees in a forest get twenty percent more. Cap the maximum probability at ninety-five percent. Count how many houses have a probability over seventy percent. Return this count and the average probability of all houses. Example: 38mm hole, 2 meters high, in a field yields high probability.

title: Solar Filter Exposure Timer
spec: Write a function `time(observations)` that receives an array of viewing session arrays, each containing the optical density of the solar filter, the current UV index, and the observer age. Determine the maximum safe continuous viewing time in minutes. First, calculate the base transmission percentage by taking ten to the power of negative optical density. For a safe solar filter with an optical density of five, this is extremely small. The base safe time is one divided by the transmission percentage, divided by ten thousand, which typically gives around one hundred minutes for a standard filter. If the UV index is above eight, reduce this time by thirty percent. If the index is between five and eight, reduce it by ten percent. Consider the observer age: children under twelve have more sensitive eyes, so reduce their permitted time by fifty percent. Seniors over sixty get a twenty percent reduction. Sum the safe viewing times for all sessions. Return an array with the total safe time across sessions and the shortest individual session time. Example: density 5, UV 9, age 10 gives heavily restricted time.

title: Celestial Meridian Transit
spec: Write a function `transit(measurements)` to calculate star transit times. Input is a list of four numbers: julian date, observer longitude in degrees, right ascension in hours, and declination in degrees. First, calculate the greenwich sidereal time by taking the julian date, subtracting two million four hundred fifty one thousand five hundred forty five, and multiplying by twenty four. Convert observer longitude to hours by dividing by fifteen. Add the observer longitude in hours to the greenwich sidereal time to get the local sidereal time. Find the hour angle by subtracting the right ascension from the local sidereal time. If the hour angle is negative, add twenty four to normalize it. Calculate maximum altitude by subtracting the absolute difference between latitude and declination from ninety. Return a list of the hour angle and maximum altitude. Example: input [2459000.5, 45, 12, 45] -> output [18.2, 70.0].

title: Circuit Board Trace
spec: Write a function `trace(parameters)` to calculate required copper widths. Input is a list containing current in amps, allowable temperature rise in degrees celsius, and copper thickness in ounces. If the current is zero, immediately return a list of two zeros. If the copper thickness is strictly less than zero point five ounces, return an error string. Ensure the allowable temperature rise is at least ten degrees; if lower, override it to ten degrees for safety. Multiply the current by the inverse of a base constant of zero point zero four eight, raise that result to the power of one divided by zero point four four, and divide by the temperature rise raised to the power of zero point four four to find internal cross sectional area. To find the internal width in mils, divide this area by the copper thickness multiplied by one point three seven eight. For external width, repeat the area calculation but use a larger base constant of zero point zero six four, then convert to width using the same method. Return a list of the internal width and external width.

title: Shoe Sizing Converter
spec: Write a function `shoes(length)` to convert foot length into global standards. Input is foot length in centimeters. If the original length is less than ten or greater than forty, return an empty list immediately to indicate an invalid measurement. First, calculate the mondopoint size by multiplying the length by ten and rounding to the nearest five millimeters. Next, compute the european size by dividing the length by zero point six six seven and adding one point five, rounding to the nearest half size. For the uk size, multiply the length by three, divide by two point five four to convert to inches, subtract twenty five, and round to the nearest half size. Check if the computed uk size is negative, and if so, reset it to zero. Find the united states men size by adding one to the uk size. Find the united states women size by adding two to the uk size. Return a list containing mondopoint, european, uk, us men, and us women sizes.

title: Caravan Towing Match
spec: Write a function `tow(specs)` to evaluate towing safety. Input is a list of vehicle weight, gross combined mass, max tow limit, max tow ball limit, caravan empty weight, and caravan payload. If the vehicle weight is zero, return an error string. If the caravan empty weight is strictly greater than the maximum tow limit, it is unsafe even before adding payload, so fail the check early. Calculate the total caravan weight by adding its empty weight and payload. Verify that the total caravan weight does not exceed the maximum tow limit. Next, calculate the estimated tow ball weight, which is exactly ten percent of the total caravan weight, and check that this is less than or equal to the maximum tow ball limit. Finally, ensure the vehicle weight plus total caravan weight does not exceed the gross combined mass limit. If all checks pass, return the string safe. If any check fails, return a list of strings describing which specific limits were exceeded.

title: Water Purifier Filter Life
spec: Write a function `filter(data)` to simulate usage over time. Input is the initial filter capacity in gallons and a list of daily usage records, where each record contains gallons used, a turbidity rating string, and a chlorine rating string. If the initial capacity is less than or equal to zero, return zero days immediately. Iterate through each day of usage. If the turbidity rating is high, multiply that day's gallons by one point five because sediment clogs the filter pores faster. Keep a count of consecutive days with high turbidity; if it reaches three days in a row, reduce the total remaining capacity by an extra ten gallons due to severe clogging. If the chlorine rating is high, multiply the daily gallons by one point two to account for activated carbon depletion. Subtract the adjusted daily usage from the total capacity. If the capacity drops to zero or below, stop and return the number of days the filter lasted. If all records are processed and capacity remains, return the remaining capacity rounded to one decimal place.

title: Lens Depth of Field
spec: Write a function `focus(settings)` to compute optical distances. Input is a list containing focal length in millimeters, aperture f-number, subject distance in meters, and circle of confusion in millimeters. First, compute the hyperfocal distance in meters by squaring the focal length and dividing by the product of the aperture, the circle of confusion, and one thousand. Calculate the near limit of acceptable focus by multiplying the hyperfocal distance by the subject distance, and dividing that by the hyperfocal distance plus the subject distance minus the focal length in meters. Calculate the far limit similarly, but subtract the subject distance in the denominator instead of adding it. If the denominator for the far limit is zero or negative, set the far limit to negative one to indicate an infinite far distance. Return a list containing the hyperfocal distance, near limit, and far limit. Example: input [50, 8, 5, 0.03] -> output [10.4, 3.4, 9.5].

title: Portable Device Runtime
spec: Write a function `runtime(specs)` to estimate battery duration. Input is a list containing battery capacity in milliamp hours, active current draw, sleep current draw, active minutes per hour, and a power supply efficiency percentage. If the battery capacity is exactly zero, return an error string immediately. If the active minutes per hour exceed sixty, cap them at exactly sixty. The power supply efficiency must be between one and one hundred; if it is outside this range, default it to ninety percent. Convert the active minutes to a fraction of an hour by dividing by sixty. Calculate the average current draw by multiplying the active current by the active fraction, and adding the sleep current multiplied by the remaining inactive fraction. Apply the power supply efficiency by multiplying the average current by one hundred and dividing by the efficiency percentage. Divide the total battery capacity by the adjusted average current to find the total runtime in hours. Return a list of two integers representing whole days and remaining whole hours.

title: Tire Size Calculator
spec: Write a function `tire(dimensions)` to compare two metric wheel profiles. Input is a list of two tire profiles, each containing tread width in millimeters, aspect ratio percentage, and wheel diameter in inches. If either tire has an aspect ratio of zero, it is an invalid profile; return an empty list. For each tire profile, calculate the sidewall height by multiplying the width by the aspect ratio and dividing by one hundred. Convert the sidewall height from millimeters to inches by dividing by twenty five point four. Calculate the overall tire diameter by adding twice the sidewall height to the wheel diameter. Calculate the circumference of each tire by multiplying the diameter by pi. Compute the percentage difference in circumference between the second tire and the first tire. Check if the calculated overall diameter of the second tire exceeds the first tire by more than three percent; if so, append a safety warning string to the output list. Return a list of the two overall diameters, the percentage difference, and optionally the warning string.

title: Paintball Trajectory
spec: Write a function `trajectory(factors)` to estimate external ballistics. Input is a list containing initial velocity in feet per second, firing angle in degrees, crosswind speed in miles per hour, and distance to target in feet. If the initial velocity is zero, the projectile never leaves the barrel, so return a list of three zeros. If the firing angle is exactly ninety degrees, the ball is fired straight up; horizontal drift is zero, and return only the flight time until it hits the ground. Convert the crosswind speed to feet per second by multiplying by one point four six seven. Calculate the initial horizontal and vertical velocity components using the cosine and sine of the firing angle. Find the total time of flight by dividing the distance to target by the horizontal velocity. Calculate the vertical drop caused by gravity using thirty two point two feet per second squared over the time of flight. Calculate the horizontal wind drift by multiplying the crosswind speed by the time of flight. Return a list of flight time, vertical drop, and horizontal drift.

title: Server Rack Heat Dissipation
spec: Write a function `cooling(datacenter)` to determine needed thermal capacity. Input is a list containing the number of servers, average power draw per server in watts, number of network switches, and a string representing the cooling efficiency level. Calculate the total IT equipment power by multiplying the number of servers by their average power draw, and adding fifty watts for each network switch. Convert the total power from watts to british thermal units per hour by multiplying by three point four one. If the cooling efficiency string is standard, increase the cooling load by thirty percent to account for facility overhead. If the efficiency is high, increase it by only ten percent. Add an additional safety margin of five thousand british thermal units for redundant backup capacity. Return the final total required cooling capacity. Example: input [10, 300, 2, "standard"] -> output 18641.5.

title: Kayaking Paddle Length
spec: Write a function `paddle(paddler)` to find the ideal gear fit. Input is a list containing paddler height in inches, boat width in inches, and a string representing the paddling style. If the paddler height is less than forty eight inches, return a base youth size of one hundred fifty centimeters without further adjustments. Start with a base paddle length of two hundred centimeters. For every full inch of paddler height strictly over sixty inches, add one centimeter to the base length. For every full inch of boat width strictly over twenty four inches, add two centimeters. Adjust for the paddling style: if the style is high angle, subtract five centimeters because the paddle is held closer to vertical. If the style is low angle, add five centimeters to accommodate a more relaxed, horizontal stroke. If the boat width is wider than thirty six inches, it is considered a specialized craft, so add an extra ten centimeters to the final calculated length. Return the final recommended paddle length in centimeters.

title: Coffee Extraction Yield
spec: Write a function `extraction(brew)` to evaluate beverage quality. Input is a list containing dry coffee weight in grams, total brewed liquid weight in grams, and the total dissolved solids percentage read from a refractometer. If the total brewed liquid weight is strictly less than the dry coffee weight, it is physically impossible, so return an error string. If the refractometer reading is exactly zero, assume no extraction occurred and return a list containing a zero yield and a quality string of unextracted. Calculate the total mass of the dissolved coffee solids by multiplying the liquid weight by the dissolved solids percentage and dividing by one hundred. Calculate the extraction yield percentage by dividing the dissolved coffee mass by the dry coffee weight and multiplying by one hundred. Determine the extraction quality based on the yield. If the yield is strictly under eighteen percent, the quality is under-extracted. If it is strictly over twenty two percent, the quality is over-extracted. Otherwise, it is ideally extracted. Return a list with the yield percentage and the quality string.

title: Pendulum Clock Calibration
spec: Write a function `pendulum(settings)` to compute timing corrections. Input is a list containing current pendulum length in meters, the target time period in seconds, and the current measured time period in seconds. If the measured time period is exactly zero, return an error string to prevent division by zero. First, calculate the acceleration due to gravity locally by multiplying the length by four times pi squared, and dividing by the square of the current measured time period. Next, determine the ideal pendulum length needed to achieve the target time period using this calculated local gravity. Square the target period, multiply by the local gravity, and divide by four times pi squared. Finally, calculate the required adjustment amount by subtracting the current length from the ideal length. If the adjustment is less than zero point zero zero one meters in either direction, set the adjustment to exactly zero to indicate it is within tolerance. Return a list of the ideal length and the required adjustment in meters.

title: Drone Payload Capacity
spec: Write a function `payload(drone)` to estimate lifting capabilities. Input is a list containing total combined motor thrust in grams, empty frame weight, battery weight, and onboard camera weight. Sum the frame, battery, and camera weights to find the baseline dry weight of the drone. If the total motor thrust is less than the dry weight, it cannot fly at all, so return a list of two zeros. Determine the maximum safe takeoff weight for agile flight by multiplying the total thrust by zero point five. Determine the maximum safe takeoff weight for gentle hovering by multiplying total thrust by zero point seven. Subtract the dry weight from the agile takeoff weight to find the available payload capacity for agile maneuvering. Subtract the dry weight from the hovering takeoff weight to find the available payload for gentle hovering. If the camera weight alone exceeds five hundred grams, it is considered heavy payload; subtract an additional fifty grams from both final payload capacities to account for upgraded mounting hardware. Return a list containing the agile payload and hover payload capacities in grams.

title: Satellite Dish Pointing
spec: Write a function `pointing(location)` to calculate aiming angles. Input is a list containing the satellite longitude in degrees, the receiver latitude in degrees, and the receiver longitude in degrees. First, calculate the difference in longitude between the satellite and the receiver. If the receiver latitude is exactly zero, the receiver is on the equator, requiring a simplification: the elevation relies only on the longitude difference. Convert all angles to radians. Calculate the azimuth angle by taking the arctangent of the tangent of the longitude difference divided by the sine of the receiver latitude. Calculate the elevation angle using the arccosine of the product of the cosine of receiver latitude and the cosine of the longitude difference. Convert the calculated azimuth and elevation back to degrees. Adjust the azimuth to represent a compass heading by subtracting it from one hundred eighty degrees if the receiver is in the northern hemisphere. If the calculated elevation angle is negative, the satellite is below the horizon; return an empty list to indicate no line of sight. Return a list of the elevation and the compass azimuth.

title: Scuba Decompression Stop
spec: Write a function `dive(profile)` to calculate surfacing schedules. Input is a list containing the maximum dive depth in meters and the total bottom time in minutes. First, ensure the maximum depth is strictly greater than zero; if not, return an empty list. Next, verify the bottom time is not negative. Calculate a tissue nitrogen loading factor by multiplying the depth by the bottom time. If the loading factor is less than five hundred, no mandatory decompression stops are needed, so return an empty list. If the factor is between five hundred and eight hundred inclusive, a standard safety stop of three minutes at five meters depth is required. If the loading factor is strictly greater than eight hundred, a deep stop is required: calculate half the maximum depth and schedule a two-minute stop there, followed by a standard five-minute stop at five meters. Return a list of lists, where each inner list contains a stop depth and its duration in minutes. Example: input [30, 30] -> output [[15, 2], [5, 5]].

title: Bicycle Chain Length
spec: Write a function `chain(bike)` to determine drivetrain requirements. Input is a list containing chainstay length in inches, number of teeth on the largest front chainring, and number of teeth on the largest rear cog. If the chainstay length is less than ten inches, it is unusually short; return an error string. First, multiply the chainstay length by two to account for the upper and lower runs of the chain. Add the number of front teeth and rear teeth together, and divide their sum by two to estimate the chain wrapping around half of each gear. Add this gear wrap value to the doubled chainstay length. If the front chainring has fewer teeth than the rear cog, this is a highly unusual negative gear ratio, but proceed with the calculation anyway while adding four extra inches for safety. Finally, add two standard extra inches to accommodate the tensioning pulleys of the rear derailleur. Since a bicycle chain can only be joined in whole pairs of inner and outer plates, round the total length up to the nearest even whole number. Return the required number of chain links.

title: Sauna Heater Sizing
spec: Write a function `heater(room)` to compute thermal generation needs. Input is a list containing room length, width, height in feet, and the total area of uninsulated materials like glass or stone in square feet. Verify that the total area of uninsulated materials does not exceed the total surface area of the room walls and ceiling; if it does, return an error string. First, calculate the base room volume in cubic feet by multiplying length, width, and height. If the calculated base volume is less than fifty cubic feet, no heater is required, so return a zero. For every square foot of uninsulated material, add one point two cubic feet to the base volume to account for heat loss. If the sauna has an all-glass door, add an additional ten cubic feet to the adjusted volume. Finally, divide the total adjusted volume by fifty to determine the required heater power in kilowatts. If the total volume is over five hundred cubic feet, return a list containing half the required power twice, recommending two heaters. Otherwise, return a list with the single required power.

title: Woodworking Jointer Setup
spec: Write a function `jointer(machine)` to calculate optimal milling parameters. Input is a list containing cutterhead rotation speed in revolutions per minute, number of knives installed on the cutterhead, and the target surface finish measured in cuts per inch. If the cutterhead rotation speed is exactly zero, the machine is off, so return a list of two zeros. If the number of knives is exactly one, the cutterhead is severely unbalanced; return an error string. Calculate the total number of cuts made per minute by multiplying the rotation speed by the number of knives. Calculate the required board feed speed in inches per minute by dividing the total cuts per minute by the target cuts per inch. Convert this feed speed into feet per minute by dividing by twelve. If the feed speed exceeds thirty feet per minute, it is considered unsafe for manual feeding. If the calculated feed speed is strictly less than five feet per minute, wood will burn due to friction; append a burn warning string to the output. Return a list containing the feed speed in feet per minute and a boolean indicating if it is safe to hand feed.

title: Guitar Fret Spacing
spec: Write a function `frets(instrument)` to compute fretboard geometry. Input is a list containing the open scale length of the instrument in millimeters and the total number of frets to calculate. If the total number of frets is zero or negative, return an empty list. If the open scale length is strictly less than two hundred millimeters, it is too short to be a standard instrument; return an error string. The mathematical constant for equal temperament fret placement is the twelfth root of two, which is approximately one point zero five nine four six. For each fret number from one up to the total, calculate its exact distance from the nut. The remaining string length for any fret is found by dividing the previous remaining length by the temperament constant. The distance from the nut is the original open scale length minus this new remaining length. Stop calculating and return the list early if any individual fret distance exceeds the scale length. Keep a running list of distances from the nut for each fret position. Return the list of distances rounded to one decimal place.

title: Ski Binding DIN
spec: Write a function `binding(skier)` to determine release tension. Input is a list containing skier weight in kilograms, height in centimeters, age in years, boot sole length in millimeters, and a skier type integer of one, two, or three. If the skier weight is strictly under thirteen kilograms, they are too light for adult bindings; return an error string. If the boot sole length is strictly under two hundred millimeters, it is incompatible with standard adult bindings, so return a zero. Calculate a base release value by dividing the weight by ten. If the height is strictly less than one hundred fifty centimeters, reduce the base value by one. If the age is strictly over fifty or strictly under ten, reduce the value by one. Adjust for skier type: if type two, increase the value by one; if type three, increase by two. If the boot sole length is strictly greater than three hundred thirty millimeters, subtract zero point five to compensate for the longer leverage. Ensure the final release value is capped at a maximum of eighteen. Return the final setting rounded to the nearest half step.

title: Rocket Nozzle Expansion
spec: Write a function `nozzle(engine)` to optimize thrust geometry. Input is a list containing combustion chamber pressure, ambient atmospheric pressure, and the specific heat ratio of the exhaust gases. First, if the atmospheric pressure is exactly zero, return an error string to avoid division by zero in the void of space. Calculate the pressure ratio by dividing the chamber pressure by the atmospheric pressure. Calculate an exhaust velocity factor by taking the pressure ratio, raising it to the power of the specific heat ratio minus one divided by the specific heat ratio, and subtracting this from one. Calculate the throat area multiplier by taking the inverse of the specific heat ratio. Combine these factors to find the optimal exit area ratio that perfectly expands the exhaust flow to match the ambient atmospheric pressure without under or over expanding. If the calculated ratio is less than one, force it to exactly one, as converging nozzles are a separate domain. Return the optimal expansion ratio rounded to two decimal places.

title: Pool Chemical Dosing
spec: Write a function `pool(test)` to balance water chemistry. Input is a list containing pool volume in gallons, current pH level, and current alkalinity in parts per million. If the pool volume is less than one thousand gallons, it is too small for standard dosing; return an empty list. If the initial pH is perfectly seven point four and alkalinity is exactly one hundred, no chemicals are needed, so return a list of three zeros. First, evaluate the alkalinity. For every ten parts per million the alkalinity is strictly below the ideal level of one hundred, calculate one point five pounds of baking soda per ten thousand gallons of pool volume. Next, evaluate the pH level. If the pH is strictly over seven point six, calculate twelve ounces of muriatic acid per ten thousand gallons for every zero point two drop needed to reach seven point four. If the pH is strictly under seven point two, calculate six ounces of soda ash per ten thousand gallons for every zero point two increase needed. Return a list containing pounds of baking soda, ounces of acid, and ounces of soda ash.

title: Asphalt Driveway Paving
spec: Write a function `paving(driveway)` to estimate material logistics. Input is a list containing driveway length in feet, width in feet, and desired asphalt thickness in inches. If the driveway length or width is zero, return a list of two zeros. If the desired thickness is strictly less than two inches, it is too thin for structural integrity, so return an error string. Convert the thickness to feet by dividing by twelve. Calculate the total required volume in cubic feet by multiplying length, width, and thickness. Convert the volume from cubic feet to cubic yards by dividing by twenty seven. Add a ten percent allowance for uneven subgrade and edge compaction by multiplying the volume by one point one. Asphalt density is typically two point zero five tons per cubic yard; multiply the adjusted cubic yards by this density to find the total tons of asphalt required. A standard dump truck holds exactly fifteen tons. Divide the total tons by fifteen and round up to find the number of truckloads. If the total tons calculated is less than one, default the required truckloads to exactly one. Return a list containing total tons and truckloads.

title: Lawn Sprinkler System
spec: Write a function `sprinkler(yard)` to design an irrigation layout. Input is a list containing yard length in feet, width in feet, water supply pressure in pounds per square inch, and available flow rate in gallons per minute. If the water supply pressure is strictly less than thirty pounds per square inch, the rotors will not pop up; return a list of two zeros. If the available flow rate is strictly less than three gallons per minute, even a single rotor cannot be powered, so return a list of two negative ones. Calculate the total yard area in square feet. A standard pop up rotor covers a circular area with a radius of twenty feet. Calculate the effective coverage area of one rotor using pi times the radius squared. Determine the minimum number of rotors needed by dividing the total yard area by the rotor coverage area, rounding up to the nearest whole number. Each rotor consumes exactly three gallons per minute. Calculate the total required flow by multiplying the number of rotors by three. Divide the total required flow by the available flow rate to determine the number of distinct watering zones needed, rounding up. Return a list of rotors and zones.

title: Synthesizer Oscillator Detune
spec: Calculate the frequency of a secondary synthesizer oscillator given detune parameters. The entry function `detune(settings)` receives a list containing the base frequency in hertz, the detune amount in cents, an analog drift factor from zero to ten, and a waveform identifier where one is sine and two is saw. First, calculate the ideal detuned frequency by multiplying the base frequency by two raised to the power of the detune cents divided by twelve hundred; next, apply the analog drift by multiplying the drift factor by zero point zero five and adding that percentage to the ideal frequency. If the waveform is a saw wave, subtract two hertz to account for phase cancellation at the attack stage, and if the base frequency is below one hundred hertz, add a bass boost correction by increasing the frequency by one percent. Finally, if the total calculated frequency exceeds twenty thousand hertz, cap it at twenty thousand to remain within human hearing. Return the final frequency rounded to three decimal places.

title: Mechanical Keyboard Lube Volume
spec: Determine the total milliliters of switch lubricant required for a custom mechanical keyboard build. The function `lubricate(build)` takes a list with the number of switches, the switch type where one is linear and two is tactile, a spring weight in grams, and an application style where one is thin and two is thick. The base volume is zero point zero five milliliters per switch, but if the application style is thick, increase the per switch volume by zero point zero two milliliters. For tactile switches, decrease the total calculated volume by ten percent to avoid losing the tactile bump; additionally, if the spring is heavier than sixty five grams, add an extra zero point zero one milliliters per switch to coat the larger springs. Calculate the overall total volume by multiplying the adjusted per switch volume by the number of switches, then add a flat one milliliter buffer to the overall total for product lost in the brush. If the final amount is under three milliliters, round up to exactly three, and return the final volume rounded to one decimal place.

title: Bonsai Wire Thickness
spec: Calculate the required aluminum wire thickness in millimeters to bend a bonsai branch. The function `wire(branch)` accepts a list containing the branch diameter in millimeters, a wood hardness score from one to five, the bending angle in degrees, and a season indicator where one is spring and zero is winter. The rule of thumb dictates the base wire thickness should be one third of the branch diameter. Adjust for wood hardness: for a score of four or five, increase the thickness by twenty five percent, and for a score of one, decrease it by ten percent. If the bending angle exceeds forty five degrees, add a flat zero point five millimeters for extra holding power; conversely, if the season is winter, the wood is brittle, so subtract zero point two millimeters to enforce a gentler bend. If the resulting wire thickness is greater than six millimeters, divide the thickness by two and return a list containing the word single in quotes replaced by the word double and the halved thickness, indicating two wires must be used. Otherwise, return a list with the word single and the final thickness, rounding all numeric outputs to one decimal place.

title: Medieval Trebuchet Range
spec: Estimate the firing range of a medieval trebuchet in meters based on its physical properties. The function `siege(weapon)` processes a list containing the counterweight mass in kilograms, the projectile mass in kilograms, the sling length in meters, and a pivot friction percentage. First, find the mass ratio by dividing the counterweight mass by the projectile mass, then calculate the theoretical energy by multiplying the mass ratio by the sling length. The base range is this energy multiplied by a constant of two point five; from this, subtract the pivot friction percentage directly from the base range. If the projectile mass is over fifty kilograms, subtract an additional ten meters for air drag, and if the sling length is greater than three meters, add a fifteen percent efficiency bonus to the current range. Finally, if the mass ratio is less than fifty, apply a stall penalty by reducing the total range by twenty percent. Ensure the final range does not drop below zero, capping it there if necessary, and return the estimated range rounded to the nearest integer.

title: Tattoo Ink Dilution
spec: Compute the drops of distilled water needed to dilute black tattoo ink for a gray wash shading technique. The function `wash(ink)` takes a list with the initial black ink drops, the target shade percentage from ten to ninety, the skin tone darkness from one to ten, and a needle configuration where one is liner and two is magnum. Calculate the required total drops by dividing the initial ink drops by the target shade percentage expressed as a decimal, making the base water drops equal to the total drops minus the initial ink drops. Adjust for the needle: if using a magnum needle, increase the water drops by twenty percent because magnums saturate more heavily. Next, consider the skin tone: for a tone of seven or higher, subtract three drops of water to keep the pigment dark enough to show against the skin; if the target shade is below twenty percent, add five extra drops of water to ensure a buttery smooth fade. If the calculated water drops fall below zero, set them to zero, and return the final water drops rounded to the nearest whole number.

title: DJ Set Transition Energy
spec: Calculate the perceived energy level change during a DJ transition between two tracks. The function `transition(tracks)` receives a list of four numbers: outgoing track tempo in beats per minute, incoming track tempo in beats per minute, a key compatibility score from one for perfect to four for dissonant, and the incoming track base energy from one to ten. First, calculate the tempo difference by subtracting the outgoing tempo from the incoming tempo, then multiply this difference by zero point five to get the tempo energy shift, adding this shift to the incoming base energy. Apply the key compatibility penalty: subtract zero for a score of one, one for a score of two, two for three, and three for four. If the tempo difference is greater than ten beats per minute, subtract an additional one point five from the total to account for dancefloor confusion. If the final energy level exceeds ten, cap it at ten, and if it drops below one, cap it at one. Return a list containing a boolean indicating if the transition is smooth, meaning the tempo difference was less than five and key score was one or two, followed by the final energy level rounded to one decimal place.

title: Fireworks Mortar Lift Charge
spec: Determine the grams of black powder needed to lift an aerial firework shell safely into the sky. The function `charge(shell)` receives a list containing the shell diameter in inches, the shell weight in grams, a powder quality factor from zero point eight to one point two, and a wind speed in meters per second. The base lift charge is one twelfth of the shell weight, which is then adjusted for powder quality by dividing the base charge by the quality factor. Evaluate the shell diameter: if the diameter is greater than four inches, add a bulk mass penalty of ten percent to the current charge; if the diameter is exactly two inches, subtract five grams because small shells launch more easily. If the shell weight is under fifty grams, subtract a lightweight deduction of two grams, and for wind above five meters per second, add five percent to the powder charge to ensure a higher break altitude. Finally, if the final calculated powder exceeds one hundred grams, apply a safety limit by capping the charge at exactly one hundred grams, returning the final powder weight rounded to two decimal places.

title: Blacksmithing Steel Tempering
spec: Calculate the hold time in minutes for tempering a carbon steel knife blade in a kiln. The function `temper(blade)` takes a list with the blade thickness in millimeters, the target hardness in rockwell c scale, the kiln temperature in celsius, and an alloy type where one is simple carbon and two is high alloy. The base time is thirty minutes per millimeter of thickness, but if the target is below sixty rockwell c, increase the time by fifteen minutes to soften the steel further. If the kiln temperature is above two hundred degrees celsius, reduce the base time by twenty percent due to faster heat saturation. Check the alloy type: high alloy steels require a soak phase, so add a flat forty five minutes to the total time, and if the blade thickness is less than two millimeters, subtract ten minutes to prevent over-tempering the thin edge. Ensure the final hold time does not drop below thirty minutes, returning the hold time in minutes rounded to the nearest integer.

title: Fountain Pen Ink Flow
spec: Estimate the ink flow rate of a fountain pen in microliters per minute based on physical characteristics. The function `flow(pen)` accepts a list containing the nib slit width in millimeters, the ink surface tension in millinewtons per meter, the feed channel depth in millimeters, and a paper absorbency score from one to five. Multiply the nib slit width by the feed channel depth, then multiply by one thousand to get a base flow rate, and adjust for the ink surface tension by dividing the base flow by the surface tension and multiplying by fifty. Evaluate the paper absorbency: a score of four or five acts as a vacuum, increasing the flow rate by twenty five percent, while a score of one slows it down, decreasing the rate by fifteen percent. If the feed channel depth is greater than one millimeter, add a heavy flow bonus of three microliters per minute; conversely, if the nib slit width is less than zero point two millimeters, subtract two microliters per minute for capillary restriction. If the final flow rate exceeds twenty microliters per minute, cap it at twenty to prevent pooling, returning the estimated flow rate rounded to two decimal places.

title: Analog Synthesizer Glide Time
spec: Calculate the time in milliseconds it takes for an analog synthesizer to slide between two notes. The function `glide(notes)` takes a list with the starting midi note number, the ending midi note number, the portamento knob position from zero to ten, and a scale mode where one is linear and two is exponential. Find the absolute difference between the starting and ending midi notes to compute the base slide time, which is the note difference multiplied by ten. Multiply this base time by the portamento knob position, and if the scale mode is exponential, modify the current time by raising it to the power of one point one. If the note interval spans more than twenty four semitones, add a long travel penalty of fifty milliseconds; if the starting note is lower than midi note thirty six, increase the entire time by ten percent to allow the low frequency oscillator to catch up. If the ending note is higher than midi note ninety six, subtract twenty milliseconds because high frequencies mask the slide duration, returning the final glide time rounded to the nearest millisecond.

title: Rubiks Cube Lubricant Speed
spec: Determine the expected turning speed impact of a silicone lubricant on a speed cube. The function `lube(cube)` processes a list with the lubricant viscosity in centistokes, the amount applied in drops, the cube spring tension from one to ten, and a break in period in solves. Calculate the initial speed factor by dividing ten thousand by the viscosity, then multiply this by the number of drops to get the base friction modifier, subtracting this modifier from a theoretical maximum speed of one hundred. Adjust for the spring tension by subtracting two from the speed for every tension point above five. Account for the break in period by adding one speed point for every ten solves, up to a maximum bonus of fifteen points; if the viscosity is below five hundred, the lube is very thin, so add a flat five points for snappiness. If the final speed drops below zero, set it to zero, returning the final speed factor rounded to one decimal place.

title: Table Tennis Racket Spin
spec: Estimate the maximum spin revolutions per second a table tennis racket can generate. The function `spin(racket)` accepts a list containing the rubber tackiness rating from one to ten, the sponge thickness in millimeters, the player swing speed in kilometers per hour, and a blade carbon indicator where one is true and zero is false. Multiply the tackiness rating by the sponge thickness to get the grip coefficient, making the base spin the swing speed multiplied by this grip coefficient, divided by ten. Apply the blade carbon adjustment: if the blade has carbon, it is stiffer and reduces dwell time, so decrease the spin by twelve percent. If the sponge thickness is greater than two point zero millimeters, add a catapult effect bonus of five revolutions per second, but if the swing speed is under forty kilometers per hour, subtract three revolutions per second due to lack of brushing force. Finally, cap the maximum spin at one hundred and fifty revolutions per second, returning the estimated spin rounded to the nearest integer.

title: Vinyl Record Groove Pitch
spec: Calculate the cutting lathe groove pitch in lines per inch for mastering a vinyl record. The function `pitch(audio)` receives a list containing the side duration in minutes, the average volume in decibels, the peak low frequency energy in decibels, and a speed setting where one is thirty three rpm and two is forty five rpm. The base pitch starts at two hundred lines per inch; subtract five lines for every minute of audio over fifteen minutes. Adjust for volume: if the average volume is greater than minus ten decibels, subtract twenty lines to allow for wider grooves, and if the peak low frequency energy is above minus five decibels, subtract an additional fifteen lines to prevent the stylus from jumping. Apply the speed setting: if cutting at forty five rpm, increase the pitch spacing requirement by decreasing the lines per inch by ten percent. If the calculated lines per inch falls below one hundred, return a list containing the boolean false and the integer one hundred; otherwise, return a list with true and the final lines per inch rounded to the nearest integer.

title: Yo-Yo Sleep Time
spec: Estimate the sleep time in seconds of a modern unresponsive yo-yo based on its design. The function `sleep(yoyo)` takes a list with the yo-yo mass in grams, the bearing spin rating from one to five, the string thickness in millimeters, and a rim weight bias percentage. Multiply the mass by the rim weight bias percentage to find the inertial mass, calculating the base sleep time as the inertial mass multiplied by the bearing spin rating. Account for string friction by dividing the string thickness by zero point five and subtracting this squared value from the sleep time. If the mass is under sixty grams, reduce the sleep time by fifteen percent due to lack of momentum, and if the bearing spin rating is five, add a flat twenty seconds of sleep time for premium ceramic bearings. If the rim weight bias is greater than seventy percent, add a stability bonus of ten percent to the current total. If the final sleep time is less than zero, return zero, otherwise return the estimated sleep time rounded to one decimal place.

title: Neon Sign Transformer Sizing
spec: Calculate the required secondary voltage for a neon sign transformer. The function `transformer(sign)` processes a list with the total glass tube length in feet, the tube diameter in millimeters, the number of electrodes, and a gas type code where one is neon and two is argon. Find the base voltage by multiplying the tube length by three hundred, then adjust for the gas type: if using argon, decrease the base voltage by twenty percent because it has lower electrical resistance. Add the electrode voltage drop by multiplying the number of electrodes by two hundred and adding this to the total. Consider the tube diameter: if the diameter is ten millimeters or smaller, increase the total voltage by fifteen percent to push the arc through the narrow space, and if the total length is greater than forty feet, add a long run penalty of five hundred volts. Finally, round the required voltage up to the nearest standard transformer size, which are increments of one thousand volts, returning the final standard voltage as an integer.

title: Perfume Extraction Yield
spec: Calculate the estimated yield of pure floral absolute in milliliters using the enfleurage method. The function `extract(flowers)` receives a list containing the weight of petals in kilograms, the number of fat changes, the ambient temperature in celsius, and a flower type where one is jasmine and two is tuberose. The base yield is two milliliters per kilogram of petals; multiply this base yield by the weight of petals, then multiply the current yield by the number of fat changes divided by thirty to represent the saturation curve. Adjust for temperature: if the temperature is below twenty degrees, reduce the yield by twenty five percent due to slow oil release, and if the temperature is above thirty degrees, subtract ten percent because volatile compounds evaporate. If the flower type is tuberose, increase the yield by fifteen percent as it continues to produce oil after picking, and if the weight of petals is greater than ten kilograms, apply a large batch efficiency bonus of five percent. If the number of fat changes exceeds thirty six, subtract one milliliter from the final yield to account for absolute lost in the separation process, returning the expected yield rounded to two decimal places.

title: Custom PC Loop Coolant
spec: Calculate the total milliliters of coolant required to fill a custom water cooled PC loop. The function `coolant(loop)` takes a list containing the total radiator length in millimeters, the reservoir capacity in milliliters, the inner tubing diameter in millimeters, and the total tubing length in centimeters. Calculate the radiator volume by multiplying the radiator length by one point five, adding the reservoir capacity to this radiator volume. Next, calculate the tubing volume: square the inner tubing diameter, multiply by pi, divide by four, multiply by the tubing length, and divide by ten to convert to milliliters, adding this to the running total. If the radiator length is greater than three hundred and sixty millimeters, add a flat fifty milliliters for the dual pass end tanks, and if the inner tubing diameter is less than ten millimeters, add a flow restriction penalty of twenty milliliters. Add an air bleed buffer of ten percent to the current total, and if the total calculated volume exceeds one thousand milliliters, add an extra thirty milliliters for a secondary bleed reservoir, returning the required coolant volume rounded to the nearest whole number.

title: Fencing Epee Point Pressure
spec: Determine the actuation pressure in grams of a fencing epee point to ensure tournament legality. The function `pressure(epee)` accepts a list with the main spring theoretical weight in grams, the contact gap distance in millimeters, a dirt accumulation score from zero to ten, and a tip friction coefficient. The base pressure is exactly the main spring weight; modify the pressure based on the contact gap: if the gap is greater than one point five millimeters, add fifty grams of required pressure due to spring compression ramp, and if the gap is less than zero point five millimeters, subtract twenty grams due to hair trigger sensitivity. If the dirt score is above five, increase the total pressure by twenty percent because grit slows the travel, then multiply the current pressure by the tip friction coefficient. If the main spring weight is below seven hundred grams, add a fail warning penalty by adding one hundred grams, as weak springs behave unpredictably. Finally, if the calculated pressure is under seven hundred and fifty grams, return a list with false and the calculated pressure; otherwise return true and the pressure, rounding the numeric pressure to one decimal place.

title: Harmonica Reed Gap Tuning
